title: U.S.-China Investments Can Still Work for Americans
gist: Lee and Lu argue the U.S.-China Board of Investment created after the 2025 Busan Trump-Xi summit should pursue substantive auto-sector deals, but that the popular idea of extracting Chinese battery tech for U.S. EVs is misguided: China's edge lies in zonal electrical/electronic architecture (EEA) and plug-in hybrids, and real capability gains come from PATAC-style joint R&D institutions built through competitive bidding, as Shanghai did with GM in the 1990s.

themes.theme: Busan summit boards: investment track lagging trade

insights.claim: Of the two mechanisms created to implement the 2025 Busan Trump-Xi summit, only the Board of Trade (tariff reductions) has developed an agenda, while the Board of Investment (cross-border investment) has not, reflecting how hard investment has become amid U.S.-China rivalry.
insights.speaker: Lizzi C. Lee, Fengming Lu
insights.so_what: Investment détente is lagging tariff détente; don't price Chinese FDI into U.S. autos as imminent.

themes.theme: China's real EV edge: EEA and hybrids, not batteries

insights.claim: Access to cheaper Chinese lithium-ion battery technology would not by itself make U.S. EVs affordable; Japan and South Korea once led in lithium-ion batteries without that translating into EV leadership.

insights.so_what: Expect headline tech-transfer demands to fail; value lies in institutional R&D partnerships instead.
